analysis.one_liner: Caps House campaign spending, bans soft money, and requires public disclosure of nearly all donations.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by one member with 18 Democratic cosponsors, was referred to the House Oversight Committee on April 17, 1997 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten federal campaign finance law for House elections. It capped total campaign spending at $700,000 per House candidate per election cycle, capped party spending at $30,000 and independent spending at $25,000 per House race, and banned "soft money" — the unlimited contributions that corporations, unions, and wealthy individuals gave to national political parties. It also required disclosure of every contribution above $1 (the threshold had been $200), banned the leadership committees members used to bankroll each other, and brought ads that mention a candidate in the final 90 days of a campaign under federal regulation.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters, who would see big-money influence over House races reduced: unlimited party soft money and unrestricted outside attack spending would be cut off, and every donation over a dollar would be public. Candidates would also benefit — the bill's own findings note that most House candidates and half of winning challengers already spent $700,000 or less, so the cap was set above typical campaign costs while blocking the escalating fundraising arms race that keeps lawmakers dialing for dollars [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Caps total spending by a House candidate and the candidate's committee at $700,000 per election cycle, with adjustments for runoffs and close primaries, to end the escalating money race in House races [S2, S3].
Bans soft money — national and state party committees could no longer solicit or spend funds that evade federal contribution limits and disclosure [S2, S3].
Caps party committee spending on a House race at $30,000 and independent spending at $25,000, closing the routes around candidate limits through parties and nominally independent groups [S2, S3].
Lowers the disclosure threshold from $200 to $1, so nearly every dollar given to or spent on a House campaign would be publicly reported [S2, S3].

Bans the 'leadership committees' that members of Congress maintained outside their own campaign committees, and bars parties and officeholders from routing money through 501(c) nonprofit groups running voter campaigns [S3].

Treats ads that portray a federal candidate — including any ad naming a candidate in the final 90 days before an election — as campaign spending subject to federal limits and disclosure, closing the 'issue advocacy' loophole [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large donors and the parties that collected their money. National and state party committees would lose unlimited soft money and face a $30,000 cap on House spending; wealthy individuals, corporations, and unions would lose the soft-money conduit; big independent and issue-advocacy spenders would be capped at $25,000 per House race; wealthy self-funding candidates could no longer spend without limit; and incumbent members would lose their leadership committees [S2, S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Big donors, parties, and big spenders

drawbacks.text: The centerpiece spending caps were on a collision course with the Supreme Court: the bill's own findings acknowledge that Buckley v. Valeo (1976) disapproved mandatory spending limits, and the bill's nonseverability clause (Section 402) said that if any provision were found unconstitutional, none of the act could take effect — meaning a single court ruling could have voided the entire reform [S3].

Blanket spending caps can disadvantage lesser-known challengers who need more money to introduce themselves against established incumbents, although the bill's findings counter that half of winning challengers and half of winners in close races already spent $700,000 or less [S3].
Dropping the disclosure threshold to $1 would require campaigns and donors to report even the smallest contributions, adding recordkeeping and paperwork burdens across the board [S2, S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core aim — cutting off soft money and the explosion of campaign spending — addressed a real and documented problem: the bill's findings note congressional campaign spending rose from about $115 million in 1976 to $765 million by 1996, while turnout hit its lowest level since 1924 [S3]. But the design was legally fragile. Mandatory spending limits had already been rejected by the Supreme Court in Buckley v. Valeo, and by writing its own nonseverability clause the bill guaranteed that one adverse ruling would have struck down everything, including the uncontroversial disclosure and soft-money provisions [S3]. Later reform efforts relied on voluntary incentives rather than flat caps for this reason. As written, the bill was a bet on the Supreme Court reversing itself — a bet the backers could not know they would win.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Oversight Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. Scotty Baesler (D-KY) introduced the Federal Election Reform Act of 1997 on April 17, 1997, joined by 17 colleagues as original cosponsors — all Democrats, many of them moderates from competitive districts [S3, S4].
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on House Oversight, the committee with jurisdiction over election law [S3, S5].
The action record shows nothing after that referral — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor action — through the end of the 105th Congress on January 3, 1999 [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent members of Congress, the national and state party committees, and the large donors who funded them kept the existing system of unlimited soft money, uncapped outside spending, and undisclosed leadership funds.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Incumbents, party committees, and big donors

for.name: Rep. Scotty Baesler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 17 original cosponsors

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no Republicans signed on

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the only visible partisan signal is that all 19 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and none were Republicans.

industries.industry: National and state political party committees
industries.note: The bill bans soft money outright, caps party spending on House races at $30,000, and bars parties from soliciting funds for 501(c) groups. Parties would lose the unlimited-donor money that had become their main funding channel.

industries.industry: Large donors (wealthy individuals, corporations, and unions)
industries.note: The soft money ban and the $1 disclosure threshold would cut off the largest and least visible channel of political money, and with it the favored access to lawmakers that large contributions had bought.
Independent spending would be capped at $25,000 per House race, and ads naming a candidate within 90 days of an election would become regulated campaign spending subject to disclosure.

The bill bans members of Congress from maintaining any political committee besides their own campaign committee, shutting down the leadership PACs used to collect and redistribute money to colleagues.

A candidate's own spending counts against the $700,000 cap, ending unlimited personal spending. The bill's findings argue such spending forces opponents into ever-bigger fundraising, though the Court has treated it as protected speech.
